text: In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you.
reflection: Jesus spoke these words to His disciples when they were troubled. He had told them He was going away, and they could not imagine life without Him. So He gave them a promise: "In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you." The word mansions means dwelling places, rooms in a great household. Heaven is pictured as the Father's house, with room for all His children. And notice the tender phrase: if it were not so, I would have told you. Jesus was honest with His disciples. He told them hard truths about suffering and persecution. If heaven were not real, He would have said so. But it is real, and He is preparing a place there. Not a generic space, but a place for you. This month we will reflect on eternal hope and the promises of heaven. Begin with this assurance. There is a place prepared for you in your Father's house.
question: What troubles your heart today that the promise of a place prepared for you could calm?
prayer: Lord Jesus, in Your Father's house are many mansions, and You have gone to prepare a place for me. When my heart is troubled, let me rest in that assurance. Amen.

text: And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also.
reflection: Jesus did not only promise to prepare a place. He promised to come back for us: "And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also." The heart of heaven is not the place itself. It is the Person. Where I am, there ye may be also. Heaven is wonderful because Jesus is there. Being with Him forever is the greatest hope a believer has. And notice that Jesus Himself will come to receive us. We will not have to find our own way. He will come for us personally, like a bridegroom coming for his bride. This promise has comforted believers through every generation. When loved ones die, when life is hard, when the world seems dark, we hold on to this: He will come again. And we will be with Him. Today, let this hope lift your heart. The best is not behind you. He is coming again.
question: How does the hope of being with Jesus forever lift your heart today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You promised to come again and receive me to Yourself, that where You are, I may be also. Let the hope of being with You lift my heart today. Amen.

text: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
reflection: This may be the best-known verse in the Bible, and for good reason. It holds the gospel in a single sentence: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life." It begins with God's love, not our goodness. It describes that love by what it gave: His only Son. It opens the invitation to whosoever, anyone at all. It names the condition: believing in Him. And it promises two outcomes. Not perishing, and having everlasting life. Everlasting life is not just life that goes on forever. It is a quality of life, life in relationship with God, that begins now and continues into eternity. Jesus later defined it as knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent. This is the foundation of all our hope. Heaven, eternity, and every promise rest on this. If you have never truly believed, today is the day. If you have, give thanks for this gift.
question: How could you give thanks today for the gift of everlasting life, or receive it for the first time?
prayer: Father, You so loved the world that You gave Your only begotten Son. Thank You for everlasting life that begins now with You and never ends. I believe. Amen.

text: And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.
reflection: Jesus described Himself as the Good Shepherd and His followers as His sheep. Then He made a promise about their security: "And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand." Three strong statements. I give them eternal life: it is a gift, not something earned. They shall never perish: the promise is absolute. No man shall pluck them out of my hand: no one can snatch them away. Picture a child held securely in a strong father's hand. No one can pull them loose. That is the security of those who belong to Jesus. In the next verse, He adds that the Father's hand holds them too. We are held in two hands, the Son's and the Father's. This does not depend on how tightly we hold on. It depends on how tightly He holds us. If you fear losing your faith or falling away, rest in this. You are held in His hand, and no one can take you out.
question: Where have you been trying to hold on in your own strength instead of resting in Jesus' hand?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You give eternal life, and no one can pluck me out of Your hand. My security rests on how tightly You hold me. I rest in Your strong hand today. Amen.

text: For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.
reflection: Paul was no stranger to suffering. He had been beaten, imprisoned, shipwrecked, and rejected. Yet he wrote, "For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us." Reckon is an accounting word. Paul had done the math. He set his sufferings on one side of the scale and the coming glory on the other. And the glory was so much greater that the sufferings were not even worth comparing. This is not denial. Paul does not say suffering is nothing. He says it is nothing compared to what is coming. The glory will be revealed in us. Not just shown to us, but in us. We will share in it. Our bodies will be redeemed. Creation will be set free. All things will be made right. If you are suffering today, you are not wrong to feel it. But do the math with Paul. What is coming is far greater.
question: What suffering are you carrying that you could weigh against the glory to come?
prayer: Lord, the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed. Help me weigh my trials against eternity today. Amen.

text: Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
reflection: Romans 8 builds to one of the greatest conclusions in Scripture. Paul lists everything that might seem able to separate us from God: death, life, angels, principalities, powers, things present, things to come. And then he finishes: "Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." Height and depth cover every possible place. Nothing above us and nothing beneath us. Any other creature covers everything else that exists. Nothing in all creation can come between a believer and God's love. Not our failures. Not our fears. Not our circumstances. Not even death itself. This love is in Christ Jesus our Lord. It is anchored in what He has done, not in what we do. That is why it cannot be broken. Whatever you are facing, whatever you fear, whatever you have done, nothing can separate you from His love. Let that truth be your anchor today.
question: What fear of being separated from God's love could you lay down today?
prayer: Lord, nothing in all creation can separate me from Your love, which is in Christ Jesus my Lord. Let this unbreakable love be my anchor today. Amen.

text: But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him.
reflection: Paul quotes a phrase inspired by Isaiah to describe God's plans for His people: "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him." Our imagination has limits. We picture heaven using the best things we know: beautiful places, joyful gatherings, perfect peace. But Paul says whatever we imagine falls short. Eyes have not seen it. Ears have not heard it. Hearts have not conceived it. What God has prepared is beyond our best dreams. This verse also has a present application. Paul goes on to say that God has revealed these things to us by His Spirit. Through Christ, we already begin to taste the wisdom and goodness of God's plans. But the fullness is still ahead. If your view of the future is small or dim, let this verse expand it. God's plans for those who love Him are greater than anything you can picture. Look forward with wonder.
question: How might your view of the future change if you believed God's plans exceed your best dreams?
prayer: Lord, eye has not seen, nor ear heard, the things You have prepared for those who love You. Enlarge my hope, and help me trust that Your plans are better than my dreams. Amen.

text: O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?
reflection: In 1 Corinthians 15, Paul writes about the resurrection, the hope that believers will be raised with new bodies. As he reaches the climax, he taunts death itself: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" Death has always seemed like the ultimate enemy. It takes everyone eventually. It separates us from those we love. It seems to have the final word. But Paul speaks to it as a defeated foe. Where is your sting? A bee that has lost its stinger can buzz and frighten, but it cannot harm. Paul explains that the sting of death is sin, and Christ has dealt with sin. Death still comes, and it still brings grief. But for believers, it has lost its power to destroy. It is a doorway, not a dead end. If you have lost someone who belonged to Christ, take comfort. If you fear death yourself, take courage. Through Christ, the grave does not get the victory.
question: What fear of death or loss could you bring under Christ's victory over the grave?
prayer: Lord, O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? Thank You for Christ's victory over death. Give me comfort and courage because of it today. Amen.

text: For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
reflection: Paul was a tentmaker by trade, so he naturally used a tent as a picture of the human body: "For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens." A tent is temporary. It wears out, tears, and eventually needs to be taken down. Our bodies are like that. They age, weaken, and one day die. But Paul contrasts the tent with a building. A permanent house made by God, not by human hands. Eternal in the heavens. Notice his confidence: we know. Not we hope or we guess. We know. Paul was certain that something better awaited. For anyone dealing with illness, aging, or the limits of the body, this is good news. The tent is not all there is. A permanent home is waiting. And it is made by God Himself. Take care of your tent, but do not put your hope in it. Your true home is eternal.
question: How could knowing your true home is eternal give you heart today?
prayer: Lord, if this earthly tent is dissolved, I have a building from You, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. Thank You that my true home is with You. Amen.

text: While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.
reflection: Paul had just described how his outward body was wasting away while his inner self was renewed day by day. Then he explained how he kept going: "While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal." Where we look shapes how we feel. If we stare only at visible things, such as problems, pain, losses, and setbacks, we will be discouraged. Those things are real. But they are temporal. They will pass. Paul fixed his eyes on unseen things: God's presence, His promises, the coming glory, eternal life. These cannot be seen with physical eyes, but they are more lasting than anything we can see. This takes practice. Our eyes naturally go to what is visible. Faith trains them to look further. What are you staring at today? Lift your gaze. Look at what is eternal.
question: What passing trouble could you lift your gaze from today toward what is eternal?
prayer: Lord, help me look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. Lift my eyes from passing troubles to what is eternal today. Amen.

text: For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
reflection: Paul wrote to the Philippians from prison, unsure whether he would be released or executed. He weighed both possibilities and concluded, "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain." To live is Christ. For Paul, life was all about Jesus. Knowing Him, serving Him, making Him known. Every day was an opportunity to live for Christ. To die is gain. Death would not be loss but gain, because it would bring him into Christ's presence. Either way, Paul won. If he lived, he would keep serving Christ. If he died, he would be with Christ. Fear of death loses its grip on someone who sees it this way. And life takes on deep purpose. This verse asks a searching question. What would you put in the blank? For to me to live is what? Career? Family? Comfort? Success? Each of these can be good, but none can make death gain. Only Christ can. Let Him be your life today.
question: If you finished the sentence, for me to live is, what would you honestly write today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, for me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. Be my life today, and give every part of it purpose in You. Amen.

text: For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ…
reflection: Philippi was a Roman colony. Its citizens were proud of their Roman citizenship, even though they lived far from Rome. They followed Roman laws and customs. Paul used that idea to remind believers of their true identity: "For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ." The word conversation here means citizenship or commonwealth. Believers are citizens of heaven. We live on earth, but our true home, our true allegiance, is above. Like the Philippians living as Romans far from Rome, we live as heaven's citizens far from heaven. This shapes how we live. We follow heaven's values: love, humility, truth, and generosity. We do not hold too tightly to earthly things. And we look forward eagerly, because our Saviour is coming from there. Your passport, so to speak, is from heaven. Live today as a citizen of that kingdom, and watch for your King.
question: How could living as a citizen of heaven shape one choice you make today?
prayer: Lord, my citizenship is in heaven, from where I look for my Saviour. Let that true allegiance shape how I live, speak, and choose today. Amen.

text: When Christ, who is our life, shall appear, then shall ye also appear with him in glory.
reflection: Paul told the Colossians that their life was hidden with Christ in God. It was secure, but not yet fully visible. Then he looked ahead: "When Christ, who is our life, shall appear, then shall ye also appear with him in glory." Notice the phrase Christ, who is our life. Not just part of our life, or an important influence on our life. Christ is our life. Our identity, our future, and our hope are all bound up in Him. And because our lives are joined to His, when He appears, we will appear with Him. Right now, much of who we are in Christ is hidden. Others may not see it. We may not fully see it ourselves. We struggle with sin and weakness. But one day, it will all be revealed. We will appear with Him in glory. What God has been doing in secret will be displayed. If you feel unseen or unimpressive today, remember this. Your true glory is hidden with Christ, and one day it will shine.
question: What part of who you are in Christ are you longing to see revealed?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are my life, and when You appear, I shall appear with You in glory. Thank You that my true life is hidden with You and safe until that day. Amen.

text: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord.
reflection: The Thessalonian believers were grieving. Some among them had died, and they worried that those loved ones would miss out when Christ returned. Paul wrote to comfort them. He explained that the dead in Christ will rise first, and then those still living will join them: "caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord." Together with them. Believers who have died are not lost. There will be a reunion. Those who grieve will see their loved ones again. And the best part is in the final phrase: so shall we ever be with the Lord. Forever. Not just a visit. Not a temporary meeting. An eternal togetherness with Christ and with all His people. This is the hope that carries believers through grief. Death separates for a time, but not forever. If you have lost someone who belonged to Christ, hold on to this promise. You will be together again, and ever with the Lord.
question: Whom are you missing, and how does the promise of being ever with the Lord comfort you?
prayer: Lord, the dead in Christ shall rise, and so shall we ever be with You. Comfort my heart with the promise of reunion, and hold on to me as I hold on to this hope. Amen.

text: Wherefore comfort one another with these words.
reflection: After describing the hope of Christ's return and the reunion of believers, Paul ends the passage with a practical instruction: "Wherefore comfort one another with these words." The truths about heaven and Christ's return are not just for theological debate. They are for comfort. Paul gave them so that grieving people could encourage each other. Notice the phrase one another. Comfort is meant to be shared. We are to speak these words to each other, especially in times of loss. When someone is grieving, we may not know what to say. But we can share these promises. Christ is coming again. Those who died in Him will rise. We will be together. We will be with the Lord forever. Sometimes simply being present and speaking hope is the greatest gift we can give. Is there someone you know who is grieving today? Reach out to them. Comfort them with these words. Let the hope of heaven bring light into their sorrow.
question: Who is grieving that you could reach out to with comfort and hope today?
prayer: Lord, You told us to comfort one another with these words. Show me someone who is grieving today, and help me share Your hope with gentleness and love. Amen.

text: Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ…
reflection: Paul wrote to Titus about how God's grace teaches us to live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present world. And how do we do that? By "Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ." The blessed hope is Christ's return. Not a vague wish, but a certain expectation. And it is blessed because it brings joy. Looking for it shapes how we live now. When you are expecting an important guest, you prepare. You clean the house and get ready. The expectation affects your behaviour. In the same way, looking for Christ's appearing affects how we live today. It motivates holiness, faithfulness, and readiness. It also gives perspective. The troubles of this world are not the end. A glorious appearing is coming. The One who saved us will return in glory. Today, lift your eyes. Look for that blessed hope. Let it shape how you live while you wait.
question: How could the blessed hope of Christ's appearing shape the way you live today?
prayer: Lord, I look for the blessed hope and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ. Let that hope shape how I live and how I see my troubles today. Amen.

text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead…
reflection: Peter opens his first letter with a burst of praise: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead." Begotten us again means born again. God has given us new life. And that new life comes with a lively hope, a living hope. Not a dead hope that fades or disappoints, but a hope that is alive and growing. What makes it alive? The resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. Because Jesus rose, our hope is not wishful thinking. It is grounded in a historical event. Death has been defeated. And because He lives, our hope lives too. All of this comes according to his abundant mercy. Not because we earned it, but because God is rich in mercy. Peter wrote to believers facing hardship. Living hope was what they needed. It is what we need too. Hold on to it today.
question: Where does your hope feel weak, and how does a living Saviour make it alive?
prayer: Father, in Your abundant mercy You have given me a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. My hope is alive because He is alive. Help me hold on to it today. Amen.

text: To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you…
reflection: Peter continues by describing what our living hope looks forward to: "an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you." Earthly inheritances can be disappointing. They can be lost through bad decisions, eaten away by debt, fought over by family members, or simply spent and gone. But the inheritance God has for us is different. Incorruptible: it cannot decay. Undefiled: it cannot be stained or spoiled. That fadeth not away: it will never lose its beauty or value. And it is reserved in heaven for you. Kept safe, guarded, with your name on it. No one can take it. No economic crash can touch it. The next verse adds that we ourselves are kept by the power of God for this inheritance. Both the inheritance and the heir are protected. If you have lost earthly things, or fear losing them, remember this. Your true inheritance is safe in heaven, waiting for you.
question: What earthly security are you clinging to that cannot compare with the inheritance kept for you?
prayer: Lord, You have kept for me an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and that fades not away. Help me hold earthly things loosely, knowing my true inheritance is safe with You. Amen.

text: Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is.
reflection: John marvels at God's love, which makes us His children. Then he looks ahead: "Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is." Now and not yet. Now, we are already God's children. That is settled. But not yet do we see the full picture of what we will become. We still struggle with sin, weakness, and limitation. Yet John is certain of one thing: when Christ appears, we shall be like Him. Our transformation will be complete. And the reason is beautiful: for we shall see him as he is. Seeing Christ fully will change us fully. Just as we become more like what we gaze at, seeing Him face to face will make us like Him. If you are frustrated by your own slow growth, take heart. One day you will be like Him.
question: Where are you frustrated by slow growth, and how does the promise that you shall be like Him encourage you?
prayer: Father, I am Your child now, and when Christ appears, I shall be like Him, for I shall see Him as He is. When my growth feels slow, give me patience and hope. Amen.

text: But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city.
reflection: Hebrews 11 describes Abraham and others who lived as strangers and pilgrims on the earth. They never fully settled. They lived in tents, looking for something more. And the writer explains why: "But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city." They desired a better country. Not a better version of earth, but a heavenly one. Their hearts were set on something beyond this world. And notice God's response: He is not ashamed to be called their God. God takes pride in people who long for Him and His home. He is honoured by their faith. And He has prepared a city for them. Their longing was not in vain. Sometimes we feel like strangers here. We do not quite fit. Something in us longs for more. That longing is not a flaw. It is a sign that we were made for a better country. God has prepared it.
question: What longing in your heart might be pointing you toward the better country God has prepared?
prayer: Lord, I desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Thank You that You are not ashamed to be called my God. Let my longings point me to the city You have prepared. Amen.

text: For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
reflection: The believers who received the letter to the Hebrews had been pushed to the edges of their society. Many had lost homes and status. The writer reminded them, "For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come." No continuing city. Nothing on earth is permanent. Cities that seemed eternal, like Babylon, Rome, and Jerusalem itself, have been destroyed or transformed. Our own homes, neighbourhoods, and communities change over time. We cannot put down permanent roots in this world. But we seek one to come. There is a permanent city ahead, the city of God, which will never fall. This changes how we see loss. When we lose a home, a job, or a community, it hurts. But it reminds us that we were never meant to settle here permanently. Our true home is still ahead. It also changes how we hold things. We can enjoy our earthly homes while knowing they are temporary. Seek the city to come today.
question: What earthly thing could you hold more loosely today as you seek the city to come?
prayer: Lord, here I have no continuing city, but I seek one to come. Help me hold earthly things loosely and set my heart on the city that will never fall. Amen.

text: Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever.
reflection: Psalm 23 ends with one of the most comforting lines ever written: "Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever." Surely. David is certain. Goodness and mercy shall follow me. The word follow can also mean pursue. God's goodness and mercy are not passive. They chase after us. Every day of our lives, through green pastures and dark valleys, they pursue us. All the days of my life. Not some days. Not the easy days only. All of them. And the psalm ends with an eternal destination: I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever. The Shepherd who leads us through this life brings us home at the end. The journey ends not in darkness but in God's presence. As this year draws to a close, look back. See how goodness and mercy have followed you. Then look ahead with confidence. They will keep following until you are home.
question: Looking back, where can you see that goodness and mercy have followed you?
prayer: Lord, surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in Your house for ever. Thank You for pursuing me with goodness. Bring me home. Amen.

text: As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness.
reflection: Psalm 17 is a prayer for protection from enemies. David describes men who are satisfied with the things of this world: wealth, children, and possessions. They have their portion in this life. But David's hope is different: "As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness." As for me. David chooses a different kind of satisfaction. Not earthly abundance, but seeing God's face. And he looks forward to waking up. This may refer to each new morning, but many have seen in it a hope beyond death, awakening in God's presence. I shall be satisfied. That is a powerful word. So much of life leaves us unsatisfied. We always want more. But David says that seeing God, being made like Him, will satisfy completely. Nothing else will be needed. What are you looking to for satisfaction? Today, let David's words become yours. As for me, I will behold His face. That will be enough.
question: What have you been looking to for satisfaction that only seeing God's face could truly give?
prayer: Lord, I shall behold Your face in righteousness, and I shall be satisfied when I awake with Your likeness. Let my hope rest on seeing You. Amen.

text: And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.
reflection: The book of Daniel ends with a vision of the end of days, when the dead will rise. Some will awake to everlasting life. And then comes this promise: "And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever." The firmament is the sky. The wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens. And those who turn many to righteousness will shine like stars forever. This is a picture of eternal honour for faithful lives. Wisdom here is not merely intelligence. It is living in the fear of God. And turning many to righteousness means helping others find their way to God. Every time we point someone toward Him, through our words, example, or prayers, we are doing eternal work. Most of this work goes unnoticed on earth. But in eternity it will shine. Who can you point toward God today? Your faithfulness will not be forgotten.
question: Who could you point toward God today?
prayer: Lord, those who turn many to righteousness shall shine as the stars for ever. Give me wisdom and love to point someone toward You today. Amen.

text: He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces; and the rebuke of his people shall he take away from off all the earth: for the LORD hath spoken it.
reflection: Isaiah 25 describes a great feast God will prepare on His mountain for all peoples. And at that feast, God will do something wonderful: "He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces." Swallow up death. Death has swallowed up countless lives. But one day God will swallow death itself. It will be gone. And then a tender image: God wiping away tears from every face. Not a distant command for sorrow to cease, but the personal touch of God's own hand, gently drying our tears. Every grief, every loss, every heartbreak. He will wipe them all away. The verse ends with certainty: for the LORD hath spoken it. This is not a hopeful guess. God has said it, and He will do it. Many people carry sorrow today. Some carry losses that feel unbearable. This promise is for them. A day is coming when God Himself will wipe every tear away. Hold on to that day.
question: What tears could you bring to God today, holding on to the day He will wipe them all away?
prayer: Lord, You will swallow up death in victory and wipe away tears from off all faces. You have spoken it, and it is certain. Hold me in that hope today. Amen.

text: And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.
reflection: Near the end of Revelation, John sees a new heaven and a new earth. The holy city comes down from God, and a voice from the throne describes what life there will be like: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away." Read the list slowly. No more death. No more sorrow. No more crying. No more pain. Everything that makes life hard in this world will be gone. Hospitals will be empty. Funerals will cease. Grief will be a memory, and then not even that. The former things are passed away. The old order of suffering will be finished. This promise picks up what Isaiah foresaw and shows it fulfilled. God keeps His word across the centuries. If you are hurting today, you are allowed to feel it. But do not lose hope. A world without pain is coming. God has promised it.
question: If you are hurting today, how does the hope of a world without pain help you hold on?
prayer: Lord, You will wipe away all tears, and there shall be no more death, sorrow, crying, or pain. If I am hurting today, help me hold on to that promised world. Amen.

text: And he that sat upon the throne said, Behold, I make all things new. And he said unto me, Write: for these words are true and faithful.
reflection: Then the One seated on the throne spoke: "Behold, I make all things new." Not I make all new things, as if God would discard everything and start from scratch. But I make all things new. He takes what is broken and restores it. He takes what is old and renews it. Creation itself will be redeemed. Then He told John, "Write: for these words are true and faithful." God wanted this promise recorded so that every generation could read it and be sure. Making things new is what God does. He made the world new at creation. He makes hearts new when people come to faith. And one day He will make everything new. As this year draws toward its end, many people think about new beginnings. They make resolutions and hope for a fresh start. God's promise goes far deeper. He does not just offer a new year. He offers a new creation. Bring Him what is broken in your life today. He makes all things new.
question: What is broken in your life that you could bring to the One who makes all things new?
prayer: Lord, You said, Behold, I make all things new, and Your words are true and faithful. I bring You what is broken in my life, and I trust You to restore it. Amen.

text: And there shall be no night there; and they need no candle, neither light of the sun; for the Lord God giveth them light: and they shall reign for ever and ever.
reflection: In the final chapter of the Bible, John describes the river of life and the tree of life in the city of God. Then he adds this: "And there shall be no night there; and they need no candle, neither light of the sun; for the Lord God giveth them light: and they shall reign for ever and ever." No night. Night often represents fear, danger, sorrow, and confusion. In God's city, none of that will exist. There will be no need for lamps or even the sun, because God Himself will be the light. His presence will fill everything with brightness. And His people will reign with Him forever. We will not merely survive in eternity. We will share in God's rule. The ones who served faithfully on earth will be honoured in His kingdom. Many people know long nights, both literal and emotional. Sleepless worry. Seasons of grief. Times when darkness seems to win. But a day is coming with no night at all. God Himself will be your light.
question: What darkness, fear, or sorrow could you hold up against the promise of a day without night?
prayer: Lord God, in Your city there is no night, for You Yourself give light. Help me hold on to that promise when darkness, fear, or sorrow press on me today. Amen.

text: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal…
reflection: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus taught about two kinds of treasure. Earthly treasure is vulnerable. Moths eat fine clothing. Rust destroys metal. Thieves break in and steal. Everything we accumulate here can be lost. But Jesus said there is another option: "lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal." How do we lay up treasure in heaven? Through generosity to those in need, faithfulness in serving God, loving others, sharing the gospel, and investing our lives in what lasts. Every act of love done for Christ is a deposit in an account that can never be lost. None of this earns salvation. It is about where we put our hearts and resources. As the year comes to a close, it is a good time to take stock. What have you invested in this year? What will you invest in next year? Lay up treasure where it will last forever.
question: Where are you investing your life, and is it in treasure that lasts?
prayer: Lord Jesus, help me lay up treasures in heaven, where nothing can corrupt or steal them. Let my love and service for You be an investment that lasts. Amen.

text: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.
reflection: Paul wrote his final letter to Timothy knowing his death was near. After declaring that he had fought a good fight and finished his course, he looked ahead: "Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day." A crown was waiting for him, already set aside, laid up in storage. The righteous Judge would give it at the appointed day. Paul's life had been full of suffering, but he was not bitter. He was confident. A reward was coming. And then Paul added something wonderful: "and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing." The crown is not just for apostles or martyrs. It is for everyone who loves Christ's appearing. Everyone who longs for His return and lives in light of it. As this year nears its end, remember that faithfulness is never forgotten. The Lord sees. A crown is laid up, not only for Paul, but for you.
question: What would loving Christ's appearing look like in the way you live today?
prayer: Lord, a crown of righteousness is laid up for all who love Your appearing. Thank You that no faithfulness is forgotten. Help me live today longing for Your return. Amen.

text: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.
reflection: The very last verse of the Bible is a blessing: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen." After all the history, poetry, prophecy, gospel, letters, and visions, Scripture closes with grace. Not with a warning or a command, but with a gift. Grace is God's undeserved favour. It is how the story began, with God reaching toward a fallen world. It is how the story continues, with God forgiving, helping, and sustaining His people. And it is how the story ends, with grace resting on all who belong to Him. This is a fitting way to end a year. Whatever the past twelve months brought, gladness or grief, success or stumbling, you can close it under grace. You do not have to carry its regrets into the new year. You do not have to earn God's favour for the year ahead. His grace is already with you. Tomorrow a new year begins. Step into it the way the Bible ends: wrapped in the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.
question: As this year ends, what could you thank God for, and how could you step into the new year under His grace?
prayer: Lord Jesus, Your grace has carried me through this whole year. I close it under Your grace, and I step into the new one wrapped in it. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with us all. Amen.
